title: Child's two-sided paper: memory arrays on both wafer faces
idea: A child asks why we only draw on one side of the page. Build the cell array on the front over the periphery, bond to a carrier, thin to ~5 um, then build a second array on the backside, wired to the same sense amps and decoders through nano-TSVs (as in backside power delivery).
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; two arrays sharing one periphery layer gives ~1.6-2x bits per mm2 with no extra litho shrink.

title: Alien without lithography grows pores: anodized-alumina capacitor forest
idea: An alien that never invented lithography would grow the array. Anodize a 3-5 um sputtered Al film over CMOS so hexagonal self-ordered pores form at 25-60 nm pitch and >100:1 aspect ratio. Imprinted dimples at landing sites pin each pore over its transistor, and the pores are lined by ALD to become coaxial capacitors.
why: Reaches the AR ~115 that Fact 1 calls for with a wet electrochemical step instead of high-AR plasma etch; the capacitor layer needs no critical masks.

title: 2050 engineer slices deposited superlattice edge-on as array
idea: Deposit a 400-layer stack of alternating 8 nm channel and isolation films, dice it into bars, rotate them 90 degrees and hybrid-bond the polished cut face onto CMOS. Every film edge becomes a channel row, so film thickness sets one axis of the array pitch; the perpendicular wordlines are patterned with DUV pitch-split.
why: Takes EUV off one array axis because the pitch comes from deposition (sub-10 nm is possible); ~2-3x density at DUV cost (Fact 4).

title: Embargoed Soviet engineer prints arrays with mask-free laser interference
idea: With no EUV and no mask shop, the Soviet engineer treats the array as a crystal lattice. A 4-beam 193 nm immersion interference exposure prints the whole field's periodic hole and line grid without a mask, spacer doubling takes it to ~20 nm pitch, and one coarse KrF trim mask cuts mats and edges.
why: Takes the 3-5 array EUV layers off: a ~$5M interference tool replaces a $200M+ scanner for the most repeated layers (Fact 4, capital).

title: Farmer's alternating furrows: half-pitch-staggered tiers share vertical bitlines
idea: Farmers offset alternate furrows. In a horizontal-cell 3D DRAM, shift every odd tier by half a cell pitch so each vertical bitline pillar zippers between cells on its left and right as it climbs, serving two columns.
why: Halves the number of vertical bitline holes, or doubles their pitch, at the same bit density. This relieves the hardest 3D etch and cuts bitline coupling (Fact 2).

title: Biologist's cortical minicolumns: 16-cell bitlines with private sense amps
idea: The cortex scales by repeating short minicolumns. Split the 3D array into 16-32-cell local bitlines; a 4x4 bundle of them is muxed in the array tier onto one hybrid bond to a sense amp in a CMOS wafer below.
why: Bitline capacitance falls to ~1-2 fF, so at the same signal margin Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~1 fF. That removes the 60-75:1 capacitor (Fact 1) and enables shallow 3D tiers.

title: Islamic-tiling artist's 60-degree lattice packs cells at 3.46F2
idea: A geometric-pattern artist would never use a square grid. Put vertical-channel cells on a triangular lattice, run wordlines along one 60-degree lattice direction and bitlines along a second, and pattern both with the periodic interference or spacer flows.
why: Hexagonal packing gives sqrt(3)/2 x 4F2 = 3.46F2, ~13% more bits per area beyond 4F2 with no node shrink (Facts 4, 7).

title: Glassblower's drawn fiber: coaxial capacitors pulled from a preform
idea: The glassblower does not etch holes; they draw them. Assemble a macroscopic preform of low-melting metal cores in glass-dielectric cladding with outer metal, draw it 1000x, bundle and redraw it to ~100 nm coax pitch, then slice 5 um discs and bond them to an access-transistor wafer. Coax pitch finer than pad pitch means each pad statistically lands on at least one coax.
why: Capacitor aspect ratio becomes free: a 5 um coax with a 20 nm glass wall gives ~3 fF without any high-AR etch (Fact 1, capital).

title: Loom weaver's crosspoint: selector-capacitor cell at every thread crossing
idea: A weaver puts a knot at every warp-weft crossing. Build stackable crosspoint decks in which each crossing holds a back-to-back ovonic threshold selector in series with a thin MIM capacitor (1S1C). There is no access transistor, and holding the half-select bias minimises selector leakage during retention.
why: Each deck is 4F2 and is stacked like 3D XPoint, with no lateral transistor, the blocker named in Fact 2; ~4x density at 4 decks, if selector off-leakage can be pushed below ~10 fA.

title: Pastry chef's croissant lamination: stack-on-stack doubling of tiers
idea: Laminated dough doubles its layers with every fold. Make wafers with 8 monolithic tiers, hybrid-bond two face-to-face, thin and open vias; then bond 16-tier pairs to 16-tier pairs, mirroring orientation so the bitlines align.
why: Tier count doubles with each bond cycle: 3 cycles take 8 to 64 tiers, past the 26-tier break-even of Fact 2 without 64 sequential monolithic tiers.

title: Potter's coil: self-rolling strained membrane turns planar array into tiers
idea: The potter builds tall vessels by coiling. Fabricate a planar gain-cell array on a pre-strained SiN/Si bilayer nanomembrane and release it with a sacrificial undercut so it self-rolls into a ~20-turn scroll. Wordlines run continuously along the spiral and contacts sit only at the outer edge.
why: One planar litho pass gives ~20 effective tiers with no staircase and no per-tier masks (Facts 2, 4).

title: Shipbuilder's reusable donor hull: fifty Smart-Cut tiers per wafer
idea: Shipyards reuse the same slipway. Implant hydrogen into one thick bulk donor, bond it, cleave a 60 nm single-crystal Si tier, CMP the donor and repeat ~50 times. Each tier gets its transistors at <=450C.
why: Gives single-crystal channel tiers for 3D DRAM, and one Czochralski wafer feeds 50 tiers, cutting high-purity quartz crucible demand per bit ~50x.

title: Plumber's pipes under the floor: backside bitlines for 4F2
idea: The plumber runs pipes in the basement, not across the living room. Build 4F2 vertical-channel transistors with the capacitor on top, then flip and thin the wafer and form the bitline from the backside, contacting the pillar bottoms directly.
why: Removes the buried metal bitline in a deep silicon trench, the hardest step of 4F2 VCT; bitline capacitance falls ~30% and pitch relaxes (Facts 1, 4).

title: Termite mound chimneys: convective cooling shafts through tall stacks
idea: Termites cool their mounds with vertical chimneys. Etch dummy vertical shafts every ~200 um through the 3D array stack and fill them with a sealed two-phase working fluid (micro heat pipes) that carries heat to a top cold plate.
why: Retention roughly doubles for every ~10C cooler. Holding inner tiers ~20C cooler cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~4x and allows taller stacks (Fact 3).

title: Organ builder's tuned pipes: frequency-addressed tier selection
idea: An organ selects a pipe by its pitch. Give each tier a thin-film bulk-acoustic resonator whose frequency is set by that tier's own film thickness. One shared RF tier bus carries a tone, and only the matching tier's resonator rectifies it to turn on its select gates.
why: Replaces the staircase contact region and N tier decoders, which grow with tier count in 3D (Facts 2, 7).

title: Submariner's bulkheads: grounded shield tiers isolate hammer coupling
idea: Submarines compartmentalize so one flood does not sink the boat. Interleave a 3 nm grounded conductive bulkhead film between active tiers, and grounded shield fins between adjacent lateral wordlines in 3D DRAM.
why: Cuts wordline-to-wordline and tier-to-tier capacitive coupling and trap-mediated disturb, aiming at a row hammer threshold above 10k activations (Fact 9). Costs one deposition per tier.

title: Sculptor's lost-wax casting: inverse-opal sponge capacitor electrodes
idea: Self-assemble 30-50 nm silica spheres into a colloidal crystal as the wax, fill the gaps with TiN or Ru by ALD or electrodeposition, then dissolve the spheres in HF. Coat the interconnected metal sponge with ALD high-k and a top electrode.
why: Gives ~10x electrode area at ~10:1 height instead of 70:1 pillars (Fact 1), with no high-AR etch and no pillar collapse.

title: Crystal-growing alien: epitaxial SrTiO3 capacitors on silicon tier sidewalls
idea: A species that grows its tools as single crystals would make the dielectric epitaxial. Sr-passivate the (001) sidewalls of single-crystal Si tiers and grow epitaxial SrTiO3 by MBE or ALD with no SiO2 interlayer, against a degenerately doped Si electrode.
why: Effective k of ~70-100 meets Fact 1's 'k ~70' target and makes the lateral capacitor in 3D DRAM 3-4x shorter (Fact 2).

title: 2050 engineer's atom-thin tiers: 2D-semiconductor lateral access transistors
idea: From 2050, silicon tiers look too fat. Grow monolayer MoS2 or WSe2 by MOCVD at <=400C on each tier's dielectric to make the lateral access transistor, so a tier shrinks to ~15 nm versus ~60 nm for Si/SiGe.
why: The ~1.8-2 eV gap pushes the leakage tail well below 1 fA (Fact 3), and thin tiers allow 100+ tiers within today's etch depth (Fact 2).

title: Biologist's mitochondrial cristae: internally folded lateral capacitor
idea: Mitochondria fold their membranes to multiply area. Make each 3D DRAM tier a stack of 4 SiGe sub-layers with alternating Ge content, then use a Ge-selective lateral recess to corrugate the capacitor cavity walls before depositing the electrode and dielectric.
why: ~3x capacitor area for the same lateral length, so the horizontal capacitor shrinks and tier pitch tightens (Facts 1, 2).

title: Braille embosser's dual-relief stamp: one-imprint wordline and contact
idea: A blind reader's world is embossed, not projected. Pattern the perfectly periodic array with nanoimprint lithography from a master carrying two relief heights, so wordline trench and contact depth are defined in one dual-damascene imprint.
why: Per-layer patterning cost falls to ~1/3-1/5 of EUV, and two litho steps merge into one (Fact 4). The master can be repaired because the array has no randomness.

title: Embargoed engineer's tungsten-free wordline: doped epitaxial gate tiers
idea: Without Chinese tungsten, the embargoed engineer grows the wordline in the same epi run as the channel. A degenerately boron-doped SiGe layer in each tier is the gate, wordlines are segmented every 512 cells and strapped to copper at each segment end.
why: Removes W replacement metal from 3D arrays (tungsten chokepoint) and also drops a CVD-W module and its fill-void yield loss.

title: Skyscraper architect's sky lobbies: periphery tiers every 32 floors
idea: Tall towers use sky lobbies so no elevator runs the full height. Every 32 array tiers, insert a laser-crystallized Si or oxide CMOS 'lobby' tier holding local tier decoders and wordline drivers. Global lines only reach lobbies, and each staircase spans just 32 steps.
why: Removes the height limit on 3D DRAM (Fact 2) and shrinks staircase and periphery area (Fact 7), toward 128+ tiers.

title: Gleaner's leftover grain: restacking fab-rejected DRAM dies
idea: Gleaners collect the grain harvesters leave behind. A 10-person team buys binned-out DRAM dies (partial-bank fails, weak retention, slow bins) at scrap prices, thins them, and stacks 8 on a small base ASIC that maps out dead banks and sets per-die refresh. The stacks are sold as capacity modules for AI KV caches.
why: Turns ~5-10% of scrapped fab output into usable supply with no new wafers. Capex is a die bonder and a wire bonder.

title: Child's LEGO staircase: shingled die stack with printed edge wires
idea: A child stacks bricks in a staircase. Shingle-stack 16 thinned DRAM dies with an offset, then aerosol-jet print silver-nanoparticle traces down the stair edges to connect the stack. The tools are a ~$1M printer and die bonder a 10-person team can run.
why: Removes TSV keep-out area and the 20-30% HBM yield loss (Fact 6) for a mid-bandwidth stack of ~500 IO from two staircase edges.

title: Well-digger farmer lets chemistry dig: metal-assisted wet etch capacitor holes
idea: The farmer digs wells with water, not drills. Put a patterned Au/Pt catalyst mesh on silicon and immerse it in HF/H2O2: the silicon under the metal dissolves straight down, giving 100-200:1 smooth holes at room temperature in a beaker. ALD then lines them into trench capacitors.
why: Reaches Fact 1's AR ~115 without $50M high-AR plasma etchers, and a 10-person team can run it on a wet bench.

title: Watchmaker's water drop: capillary self-aligned die-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: Make the bond sites hydrophilic and their surroundings hydrophobic, and dispense a water droplet on each site. A die dropped within +/-50 um self-centers to <0.5 um by surface tension as the water evaporates, then direct oxide/Cu bonding is annealed.
why: Memory-on-logic hybrid bonding with a ~$200k pick-and-place instead of a $5-10M precision bonder, within reach of a small team (Facts 5, 6).

title: Astronomer's bucket brigade: CCD charge chains instead of capacitor cells
idea: An astronomer stores charge in CCD potential wells and reads single electrons at one output amplifier. Build 8-stage buried-channel charge-coupled chains in a 22-40 nm image-sensor foundry, via MPW. Each bit is ~100 electrons under one gate with no contact or capacitor, and a floating-diffusion amplifier serves every 8 bits.
why: Removes capacitor, cell contacts and most sense amps. CCD dark current gives seconds of retention (Facts 1, 3, 7), and the whole thing is made in a US/Israel CIS foundry with a fabless 10-person team.

title: Soviet engineer converts the tractor plant: NAND lines making DRAM
idea: Like a tractor factory retooled for tanks, a 10-person design team writes 1-2 mask deltas and recipe changes so an existing 3D NAND line (staircase, channel holes, tier stack) builds a vertical 2T0C gain cell. An ALD oxide-semiconductor liner replaces the poly-Si channel in the hole. The fab runs it as foundry lots.
why: Gets 3D DRAM onto already-depreciated 100+ tier tools (Facts 2, 4: depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost) without anyone building a new fab.

title: Billboard painter's giant canvas: idle display fabs print memory panels
idea: A billboard painter works big and coarse. A 10-person team designs oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays for idle Gen-6 display lines. A 1.5 m2 panel at 1.5 um rules holds ~5e10 bits (~6 GB), and it is diced into tiles bonded to logic as a slow bulk tier.
why: Uses paid-off, non-EUV display capacity for bulk working memory. Cost is projected at ~$30/GB today, falling with tighter display rules (capital, scarce EUV).

title: Open-source hacker's memory compiler for a U.S. open-PDK fab
idea: In the Linux spirit, a 10-person team publishes an open-source generator for 3T gain-cell macros boosted with stacked metal-oxide-metal capacitors on SkyWater 130/90 nm and GF 22FDX, with layout, refresh controller and characterization.
why: ~2-3x denser than SRAM and made in a U.S. fab. Moves embedded buffers off commodity DRAM and SRAM supply, and is a U.S. manufacturability win.

title: Ballroom mirror twins: one self-mating die forms a two-high stack
idea: Two identical dancers form a pair by mirroring. Design one die whose bond-face pad map is 180-degree symmetric, then wafer-to-wafer bond two identical wafers, one rotated. A mode fuse makes one die's periphery serve both arrays and power-gates the twin's.
why: A 2-high F2F memory stack from a single mask set and wafer type halves mask NRE. The bonding service is buyable by a small team (capital, Fact 7).

title: Ham radio operator's near-field link: coil-coupled stack without TSVs
idea: Ham operators talk without wires. Put 30-60 um inductive coils in the top metal of every die, glue thinned dies into a stack, and send data die-to-die by near-field magnetic coupling at ~1-8 Gb/s per coil and ~0.1-1 pJ/bit. Power comes in on edge wire bonds, and the design can be taped out on an MPW.
why: Avoids the HBM TSV area and yield tax (Fact 6) and moves data at under 1 pJ/bit (Fact 5), with packaging a small team can do.

title: Origami artist's accordion: dies folded on flexible hinges
idea: Leave N memory dies in a row on a wafer strip and thin it to 20 um. Laser-ablate the silicon between dies so polyimide/Cu flex hinges carrying the shared bus remain, then fold the strip accordion-style in a jig into an N-high stack.
why: No TSVs, no die-to-die bonding and no interposer. The bus runs through the hinges, and a 10-person team can build an 8-high stack with thinning, a laser and a fixture (Fact 6).

title: Shaker minimalist: two-mask thyristor crosspoint on purchased epi wafers
idea: The Shaker craftsman removes every unnecessary step. Buy wafers with an in-situ-doped p+/n/p/n+ epi stack from a vendor, etch line mask 1, fill, then etch perpendicular line mask 2, leaving self-aligned 4F2 thyristor pillars. Each pillar is a bistable latch with ns read and write.
why: No capacitor and no access transistor, built in a university fab with two masks; epi decks can be bonded into stacks (Facts 1, 2, 4). Holding-current standby is the cost.

title: Chef's vinaigrette separation: block-copolymer hexagonal pillar masks
idea: Oil and vinegar separate on their own. Spin-coat high-chi PS-b-PDMS, anneal it into hexagonal cylinders at 16-24 nm pitch, and guide them with a coarse 248 nm pattern (graphoepitaxy). The result is transferred into a hard mask for a 4F2 vertical pillar array.
why: Sub-20 nm pillar patterning with a spin coater, hotplate and etcher. That is EUV-free and within a 10-person team's tool budget (Fact 4).

title: Child's rubber stamp: micro-transfer printing memory dielets onto logic
idea: A child stamps hundreds of stickers at once. Release 50x50 um memory dielets from their source wafer on undercut tethers, then pick thousands at a time with a PDMS stamp and print them onto a logic wafer at +/-1.5 um placement.
why: Memory from any small fab can be printed millimetres from compute with no interposer or TSVs (Facts 5, 6). A uTP tool costs ~$1-2M.

title: Shepherd's herding dog: dielectrophoretic placement of nanowire access transistors
idea: A sheepdog drives sheep into pens. Grow doped core-shell Si nanowire transistors in bulk in a tube furnace, suspend them in liquid, and use AC dielectrophoresis on electrode pairs to herd one wire onto each site of a pre-built capacitor array.
why: Decouples a single-crystal access transistor from the capacitor substrate and removes epitaxy and transistor litho from the array. Furnace plus wet bench suits a small team (Facts 2, 3).

title: Jeweler's plating bath: electroless cobalt wordline fill replaces tungsten
idea: The jeweler grows metal from a bath. Activate the lateral wordline cavities of a 3D stack with a Pd seed and fill them bottom-up with electroless Co-B or Ru at <=70C on a ~$100k wet bench.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and the $5M CVD-W chamber from array metallization. A 10-person team can qualify the bath chemistry.

title: Home renovator's second storey: post-CMOS capacitor tier on foundry logic
idea: Like adding a storey to a finished house, buy MPW logic wafers laid out as 1T1C access arrays with exposed top-metal landing pads. In a university cleanroom, add 3 masks: 5 um oxide, holes, then ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN capacitors.
why: Puts eDRAM-class memory on any logic node without the foundry offering it, ~3-4x denser than SRAM. Capex fits a 10-person team (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Child watching dew form only on grass: area-selective ALD self-alignment
idea: Dew forms on grass, not on rock. Block the oxide with a self-assembled monolayer inhibitor so ALD Ru grows only on exposed metal. Capacitor bottom electrodes and landing pads then self-align to the contacts beneath, with no litho or overlay step.
why: Removes 1-2 critical masks and overlay-limited steps per tier (Fact 4). It needs just one ALD tool and a vapor-prime oven.

title: Baker's leavened bread: dealloyed nanoporous metal capacitor electrodes
idea: Bread rises because yeast leaves holes. Sputter a 300 nm Ag-Au or Cu-Mn alloy, dealloy it in acid to a nanoporous metal with 15-30 nm ligaments, then coat it with ALD high-k and an ALD TiN top electrode.
why: ~10-20x electrode area per footprint at 0.3 um height instead of 70:1 pillars (Fact 1). A sputter tool, an acid bath and ALD fit a small team.

title: Alien asks why the basement is empty: eDRAM inside the interposer
idea: An alien sees that the huge interposer under every AI package is passive silicon. A 10-person team designs an active mature-node interposer with deep-trench 1T1C cells, which interposers already carry as decoupling capacitors, and has a foundry build it.
why: ~2000 mm2 of otherwise wasted silicon holds ~1-2 GB of near-logic memory per package, at ~1 pJ/bit (Fact 5), with no EUV.

title: Librarian's bookshelf: memory dies standing upright on logic
idea: The librarian stores books on edge, not in flat piles. Stand 50 um thinned memory dies upright on a logic die, joined through half-via castellations made by dicing through plated vias at the die edge and soldered to the base. Coolant or air flows between the dies.
why: ~20 dies per mm of base. No TSVs and no stack-height thermal penalty (Fact 6). Dicing, plating and reflow are small-team tools.

title: Child's magnifying glass: green-laser crystallized silicon tiers over CMOS
idea: A child focuses sunlight to burn a spot without heating the whole table. Deposit a-Si at 350C on finished foundry CMOS, melt-crystallize it with a short-pulse 532 nm line laser so the transistors below stay cool, and build 2-4 tiers of top-gate poly-Si gain-cell TFTs.
why: Monolithic memory tiers over logic with a ~$1M laser and a PECVD tool (Fact 2, capital). Poly-Si leakage needs ms refresh, so it suits cache-like use.

title: Burdock-burr walker's velcro: copper nanowire room-temperature stack bonding
idea: Velcro came from burrs caught on a walker's clothes. Electroplate copper nanowire forests through track-etched polymer membrane templates on both bonding faces, then press them together at ~10 MPa so the wires interpenetrate into electrical and mechanical joints at room temperature.
why: Stacks memory on logic without nm-flat CMP, a high-temperature anneal or a precision bonder (Fact 6). A 10-person team can do it with plating and a press.
